title: Research Workshop: Dissertation Objective
text:
Steffen Lehmann opens by noting how research in urban design remains under‐theorised compared with, say, engineering or the natural sciences. He quotes the Oxford definition: “research is the systematic investigation … in order to establish facts and reach new conclusions.”
He poses the question: What constitutes “research” in the domain of urban design performance and resilience?
Because urban design is inherently interdisciplinary — combining architecture, planning, ecology, sociology, environmental engineering — the methods used must be appropriate to that complexity.
The aim of the paper is twofold: (1) to discuss and clarify what methods are appropriate when researching the performance and resilience of places in urban design; and (2) to present a conceptual framework (and practice‐based examples) illustrating how research‐informed design can operate in this field.
Thus, for your workshop, this paper gives both a “how to” (methods) and a “why it matters” (performance & resilience) for urban design research.



Lehmann outlines the methodical terrain:


He notes two broad approaches:

Research through urban design: where the design act itself becomes the research vehicle (the act of designing yields new knowledge).
Research into urban design: where the design (or place) is the object of study, and one investigates its performance or resilience.

This distinction helps practitioners and academics frame whether they are driving change via design work, or studying design outcomes.



Performance‐focused urban design research typically features:

New knowledge or new interpretation regarding how places perform (e.g., energy use, water use, comfort) rather than simply descriptive work.
Focus on measurable performance across defined criteria (resource use, environment, comfort, social functioning).
Analytical or interpretive frameworks, rather than purely intuitive or stylistic design.
Potential for scale or replication: i.e., insights that extend beyond a single building or locale.
Dissemination and peer review: so that the findings influence future design thinking and practice.

Lehmann emphasises that many urban designers and planners currently lack training in systematic data‐collection, analysis and evaluation of performance—this is a gap and opportunity.



Methodological options:
Quantitative: numerical data (e.g., microclimate readings, energy usage, water flows).
Qualitative: non‐numerical data (user interviews, observations, diaries, visuals).
Empirical research: directly from experience or observation.
He emphasises selecting the method(s) that best suit the research question and context.
In particular:

Framing a compelling research question early, based on an identified knowledge gap and literature review.
Defining aims, objectives and possibly hypotheses.
Acknowledging limitations: feasibility, data availability, scope.

Using mixed‐methods if appropriate: combining quantitative and qualitative to enrich the understanding of how a place performs and adapts. If you collect data (say in R), you should pair that with qualitative insights (surveys, interviews) to deepen analysis.




Roadmap:
Precedent and case‐study analysis: Investigate existing examples or comparable typologies to establish context or baseline.
Literature review: Identify what has been done, where gaps remain.
Glossary/key terms: Clarify terminology around performance and resilience early on.
Formulate the research question: Clearly state what you want to find out, and under what performance dimension.
Select methods: Choose the most appropriate mix and justify them.
Structure the research procedure: plan data collection, analysis, reporting.
He also reminds that urban designers, given their visual and spatial training, are well placed to organise and visualise technical data (for example via diagrams, mapping, charts) and to translate that into decision‐making tools.



Pick a place (or hypothetical neighbourhood) and outline their research question, method choice (quant/qual/mixed), and visualisation/analysis strategy.



The link between research and practice: how can research in urban design have real-world impact? He describes “practice‐oriented research‐by‐design” as a promising approach.
Different types of impact:

Scientific (knowledge creation)
Economic (business model innovations)
Environmental (reduced emissions, improved resource efficiency)
Instrumental (new policies)
Capacity‐building (skills, expertise)
Cultural/social (behaviour change)
Conceptual (adoption of new theory)

Key message: urban design research should not stay in the academic realm only—but feed back into the profession, informing design decisions, practice workflows, policy, etc.
Lehmann uses examples from leading practices (e.g., research‐driven architecture firms) to illustrate how design firms with embedded research capability can gain competitive advantage.
For those new to research, this means your methods should not just yield interesting findings—but findings that practitioners can act upon.



Performance: how well a place or neighbourhood fulfils its functions, how efficient it is in resource use (energy, water), how comfortable, healthy, accessible it is, how well it meets its design intent.
Resilience: the adaptive capacity of a place to respond to disruptions (climate change, supply chain shocks, demographic change) and recover or transform positively.
He emphasises that high‐performance urban design integrates a lifecycle perspective: resource efficiency, operational performance, durability, adaptability.


Lehmann provides examples of measurable indicators:

Energy Use Intensity (EUI) in buildings or districts (kBtu/sqm‐yr or similar)
Water Use Intensity (WUI)
Embodied carbon (kg or tonnes CO₂ e) – from material extraction, manufacture, transport, construction, decommissioning.
Operational carbon (annual emissions during use)
Access to daylight, views to nature, microclimate (shade, glare, urban heat island effect)

He also touches on more qualitative performance dimensions: user satisfaction, mental/physical health outcomes, social interaction, community well‐being.
He flags the urban heat island effect, loss of green space, and how nature‐based solutions (green roofs, walls, sustainable drainage) serve both performance and resilience aims.



Lehmann flags several practical and methodological challenges:

Post‐Occupancy Evaluation (POE) is valuable but data collection can be hindered by privacy, corporate unwillingness to share inefficiencies, user reticence.
Qualitative studies often face issues of transferability / replicability: context matters a lot, and what works for one city may not for another.
Integrating diverse disciplinary perspectives (environmental, social, technical) is still a challenge in many urban design research contexts.
The temptation remains for design to rely on intuition, aesthetics or precedent only, rather than evidence‐based performance metrics.

Lehmann argues for a shift towards more systematic, analytical, critical methodologies.



Identify such methodological threats (bias, data availability, transferability) and discuss how to mitigate them.




Project 1: A new public park on top of a freeway tunnel, reconnecting two communities through landscape and cultural facilities. Research question: How can a resource‐efficient park bring people together for community wellness? Research approach: qualitative precedent study, thematic analysis.
Project 2: An urban food hub – vertical food production & distribution centre with drone delivery port. Research question: How can urban farming and new tech create a food-distribution centre and promote sustainability, local access? Research approach: extensive precedent studies and contextual observation.
Project 3: A new gateway to the Las Vegas Arts District: a public plaza + cultural facility. Research question: How can art and architecture catalyse regeneration in the arts district? Research approach: qualitative observational data of social behaviour, interactions, spatial organisation.
Project 4: “Neo‐Metabolism”: modular micro-housing for urban infill. Research question: What is the most efficient/flexible approach for revitalising vacant sites downtown using low-carbon, off-site manufactured construction? Research approach: immersive, evolving design research process; field immersion.
Lehmann uses these to show how research questions, methods, data, design and outcomes can be combined in an urban-design studio environment. Importantly: he notes that each of these is context‐specific, and that no single study “solves” the whole problem — research is part of a continuing inquiry.


Participants must consider a comparable “mini‐design research” for their city/context.




There is a growing need for research‐led and design‐informed methods in urban design, especially given pressing challenges: climate change, urban population growth, resource constraints, health & well‐being, equity.
To address these, urban design must become more evidence-based: linking theory, method, data, design decision. He argues that the profession must shift from “creating architectural objects” to “systems thinking, research‐informed design”.
Urban designers must become lifelong learners and research‐capable professionals: willing to collect, analyse, visualise data, reflect on outcomes, iterate.
More comparative case-studies, mixed‐method research, longitudinal monitoring of performance/resilience are needed to build the evidence base for the future of urban design.
He emphasises that even good design remains a “journey of enquiry”: research does not yield final, definitive answers, but enables better questions, better understanding, better design decisions.
For your workshop, you could highlight: the takeaway here is that research methods are not optional but foundational to designing places that perform and endure.**



Research question → method → data → analysis is a chain that also applies if one uses R (or any statistical software). Although Lehmann’s examples are urban design–centric, the logic is the same, e.g., you might ask: Does a neighbourhood with higher tree canopy cover have lower surface‐temperature anomalies during heat-waves compared to similar density areas? Then you collect microclimate data, tree-canopy GIS layers, user surveys, analyse in R, visualise findings, perhaps compare multiple cities.
Emphasise mixed methods. Urban design deals with spatial, social, environmental data – so combining e.g., DTS microclimate data + user satisfaction data + GIS metrics is powerful. Your audience might feel comfortable with quantitative (R) but need encouragement to incorporate the qualitative side.
Visualisation and storytelling matter. Urban designers are good at spatial diagrams; you can link that to R’s capabilities (ggplot2, sf, raster or other apps) so that quantitative findings become actionable.
Performance/resilience metrics: some of Lehmann’s listed metrics (EUI, WUI, embodied carbon, operational carbon, heat‐island effect) can inspire variable choices or control variables in research projects (e.g., you might proxy tree cover, building density, material age, etc).
Research into place performance has relevance beyond architecture: for example, economic geographers, urban economists, sustainability analysts (which fits your subject lead role in Economics). So bridging urban design methods with economics (cost-benefit, productivity, well-being) is possible.
Real-world impact: Lehmann’s emphasis on practice‐oriented research means “how will our research inform decisions (policy, design, investment)?” This can resonate for careers in design, planning, data science, sustainability, etc.
limit scope: be realistic. Lehmann notes that research problems may be overly ambitious; he advises narrowing or breaking down into sub-problems. Good advice especially for beginners/new researchers.



Here’s a proposed flow you could use:
Introduction – hook your audience (“Why does a place perform? Can we test it?”).
Define key terms – performance, resilience, research methods (qual/quant/mixed)
Methodological framework – go through Lehmann’s roadmap: research idea → literature/precedent → research question → methods → data → analysis → reporting. Use a slide with the steps.
Metrics & measurement – discuss specific measurable variables (tree cover, energy use, carbon, user comfort) from the paper. Possibly an interactive brainstorm: what metrics would you use for your local urban place?
Case-studies review – see the four examples from Las Vegas used by Lehmann.
Common pitfalls & tips – highlight what Lehmann flags (data availability, transferability, context specificity, qualitative vs quantitative challenges).
Linking to your field – tie home to economics/Investing Club/data science: e.g., how place performance metrics might matter for real-estate investment, urban regeneration economics, sustainability investing.
Wrap-up

rigorous research in urban design matters for performance/resilience; (b) methods must be selected thoughtfully; (c) bridging design and data is essential; (d) this is relevant for emerging researchers and practitioners alike.

Q&A / reflection – invite participants to reflect on: “What surprised you from Lehmann’s framework?” or “What’s one method you might include in your next project?”

title: Welcome & Guidelines
text: Welcome to the PGR Dissertation Workshops. These sessions are user-centred and focus on the real issues Mphil researchers face while writing the dissertation — frequent questions, practical problems, and how to diagnose and improve drafts using good (and not-so-good) examples from past work at diverse universities.

text:
Workshop details & indicative content

Workshop 1 — Research Objective & Questions (7 Nov)

Research objective, research problem, rationale, and well-formed RQs.

Sample dissertations: LE471, LE400, LE468 (2017–18). :contentReferenceoaicite:9



Workshop 2 — Literature Review (30 Jan)

From objective → RQs; what a literature review is / is not. See the Literature Review workshop page.

Scope, search, read, theme, and turn reading into writing.

Dissertations: LE115, LE123, LE149, LE110 (2021). :contentReferenceoaicite:10



Workshop 3 — Methods Chapter (6 Feb)

Paradigms (positivism, realism, interpretivism), logic (inductive/deductive), designs (experiments, surveys, case study, grounded theory, ethnography, action research), cross-sectional vs longitudinal; data collection and method process.

Dissertations: LE382, LE379, LE334 (2018–19). :contentReferenceoaicite:11



Workshop 4 — Results, Conclusions, Referencing (13 Feb)

What belongs in results vs conclusions; appropriate referencing; when to move a table to the appendix.

Dissertations: LE221, LE201, LE296 (2021–22).



Workshop 5 — Drop-in & Polishing (20 Feb)

Q&A and final shaping: Introduction, Abstract, Editorial Control.

Dissertations: LE702, LE682, LE635, LE697 (2023).

title: Data Management and Methods
text:
This workshop focuses on how to write the Data Management and Methods chapter of your dissertation.
It is not a research methods lecture. Instead, it addresses the practical writing decisions examiners expect to see when assessing whether your research design is credible, feasible, and well-justified.






Core message



A strong Methods chapter answers “how” and “why this way”,
not “what does it mean.”




The Methods chapter explains how your research is carried out and why the chosen approach is appropriate for answering your research question. Its primary purpose is to demonstrate:

clarity about what data can realistically be collected,
justification for methodological choices,
awareness of the implications and limitations of those choices.

Unlike the literature review, this chapter is less analytical and more justificatory. However, it still requires judgement: different choices would lead to different types of evidence, results, and conclusions.



A useful way to think about this chapter is to move from broad to specific decisions, often illustrated through the “research onion”:

overall research approach (qualitative, quantitative, mixed methods),
data sources and collection strategies,
sampling or case selection,
analytical tools and procedures.

The key point is not to reproduce the diagram, but to show that your methods are the result of a sequence of informed decisions, not arbitrary preferences.






Practical takeaway



You are not expected to use the most advanced method available.
You are expected to use a method that is fit for your question and your data constraints.





In practice, many supervisors prefer to discuss the Data Management and Methods chapter early in the dissertation process. The reason is simple:

The data you can collect determines the questions you can credibly answer.

Starting with this chapter helps to: - clarify what is feasible within time and access constraints, - avoid designing questions that cannot be answered with available data, - ensure early alignment between objectives, data, and methods.
This workshop adopts that same logic.



Using exemplars from previous Master’s dissertations, you will:

examine how students justify their methodological choices,
identify good and weak practices in methods writing,
reflect on biases towards familiar methods,
learn how to explain limitations without undermining your project.

The focus throughout is on writing a credible Methods chapter, not on learning new techniques.






Think like an examiner



An examiner may disagree with your choices and still award high marks if your methods are clear, justified, and appropriate.

title: Data Management and Methods
section: 2.1 Exercise 2 — Method-choice bias (“methods I know” vs “methods my question needs”)
text:
2.1 Exercise 2 — Method-choice bias (“methods I know” vs “methods my question needs”)
A common weakness in Methods chapters is method myopia: choosing the method you feel comfortable with, then searching for a justification afterwards. The goal of this exercise is to recognise that bias and replace it with fit-for-purpose choice.

2.1.1 Exemplar A — Case study + multiple sources (pragmatic fit)
Source: Smart City Mission in India: case of Warangal, Methods/Data section (LE334, p. 17).

“This case study research is based on an examination of socio-economic data sets on Warangal, an analysis of planning documents, fifteen semi-structured interviews of local government officials and city residents. Both primary data and secondary data was utilised to obtain findings for the above-mentioned research questions.”

What to notice: the author commits early to multiple data sources because a single method would miss key dimensions (policy design, implementation, lived experience).


2.1.2 Exemplar B — Mixed methods + elite interviews (problem-driven choice)
Source: Indonesia’s Village Law: Policy Implementation, Research Methodology (LE379 pp. 24–26).

“To investigate the plausibility of the Village Law in meeting its main objectives, this study adopts a ‘grounded theory’, and mixed methods, case-study approach… Semi-structured, in-depth elite interviews were utilised… [to] give in-depth insights, moving beyond the accounts of existing literature, evaluations and official documents.” (PDF p. 24)


“The data collection method of the dissertation is a combination of: (i) Analysis of secondary qualitative and quantitative data… [and] (ii) Collection and analysis of primary data obtained from twenty in-depth and semi-structured elite interviews…” (PDF p. 26)


Your task (write short answers): 1. For each exemplar (A and B), explain why the decisions were made (e.g., “case study + triangulation”, “mixed methods + elite interviews”). 2. Identify weak student rationale and discuss whether it can be enhanced or discarded.






What examiners reward



Examiners reward method choice that is driven by the research problem, not by the researcher’s comfort zone.

title: Data Management and Methods
section: 2.2 Exercise 3 — Alignment + justification + relevance (methods must do work)
text:
2.2 Exercise 3 — Alignment + justification + relevance (methods must do work)
A Methods chapter should make it easy for the reader to see that each element of the design has a purpose. This is about three things at once:

Alignment: does it answer the research question?
Justification: why this method, not a nearby alternative?
Relevance: is any part of the Methods section “dead weight”?


2.2.1 Exemplar C — Why process-tracing (not “just interviews”)
Source: Indonesia’s Village Law: Policy Implementation, analysis strategy and triangulation (LE379, p. 25).

“The data gathered has been analysed via process-tracing… Process-tracing is an appropriate tool in theory testing and theory development… Patterns within the answers of interviewees were matched… and were then triangulated with secondary data.” (PDF p. 25)



2.2.2 Exemplar D — Why GIS + planning documents (not “data for data’s sake”)
Source: Smart City Mission in India: case of Warangal, data sources and analytical tools (LE334 p. 17).

“These documents have been collected to analyse… the way authorities are making an effort to utilise such ‘Smart’ solutions… The data… is analysed digitally with the help of Geographic Information System (GIS) software such as QGIS and Google Earth. Maps… assisted in comprehending the variations… and helped the researcher attain a precise geographical perspective…”


Your task (table + short paragraph):
Create a mini mapping table for one of the exemplars (C or D):









Method element
What question/decision it answers
Why this (justification)
What would be irrelevant here?

title: Data Management and Methods
text:
2.3 Typical weak Methods writing






Warning



Students often describe their tools (e.g., “I used interviews”, “I used GIS”) but do not explain what those tools allow them to conclude and what they cannot conclude.

title: Data Management and Methods
section: 2.4 Exercise 4 — Sampling FAQ (qualitative, quantitative, and the “special case”)
text:
2.4 Exercise 4 — Sampling FAQ (qualitative, quantitative, and the “special case”)
Most dissertations on this programme involve interviews (often semi-structured). Some use surveys. Others use documentary/policy sources. The sampling logic must be explicit because sampling determines what your evidence can and cannot speak about.

2.4.1 4.1 Qualitative interviews (typical pattern on the programme)

2.4.1.1 Exemplar E — Non-probability / snowball sampling (with limitations)
Source: Indonesia’s Village Law: Policy Implementation, sampling rationale (PDF p. 25). fileciteturn2file0

“The most appropriate sampling procedures were those identifying the key political actors… This led to ‘non-probability’ sampling… A snowball/chain-referral sampling… was predominantly utilised… as the population of interest was not fully visible at the initial stage of the fieldwork…” (PDF p. 25)


“Non-probability sampling also has limitations… [it] will not be representative… To address this, the selection of initial interviewees… was diversified…” (PDF p. 25)


FAQ prompts (answer in bullets): - When is snowball sampling defensible? - What is the main risk (in plain English)? - What is one credible mitigation strategy? Is saturation point used as a vague invocation?

title: Data Management and Methods
text:
2.5 4.1 Qualitative interviews: sampling FAQs (answered)

2.5.1 Exemplar — Non-probability / snowball sampling (with limitations)
Source: Indonesia’s Village Law: Policy Implementation, sampling rationale (PDF p. 25).

“The most appropriate sampling procedures were those identifying the key political actors… This led to ‘non-probability’ sampling… A snowball/chain-referral sampling… was predominantly utilised… as the population of interest was not fully visible at the initial stage of the fieldwork…” (p. 25)


Below are practical answers to the most common sampling questions that arise when writing interview-based Methods chapters.

2.5.2 FAQ 1 — When is snowball sampling defensible?
Snowball sampling is defensible when: - the population of interest is not fully observable ex ante (e.g. elites, informal actors, practitioners), - access depends on gatekeepers or professional networks, - the research aims to understand processes, experiences, or mechanisms, rather than estimate population parameters.
In these cases, the goal is informational richness, not statistical representativeness.


2.5.3 FAQ 2 — What is the main risk (in plain English)?
The main risk is selection bias: - interviewees may refer you to people who think similarly, - dissenting or marginal voices may be under-represented.
This limits the scope of claims you can make. It does not invalidate the research, provided the limitation is acknowledged.


2.5.4 FAQ 3 — What does “saturation” mean in practice?
In Master’s dissertations, thematic saturation refers to the point at which: - additional interviews no longer generate substantively new themes, explanations, or mechanisms relevant to the research question.
Saturation is not: - a fixed number of interviews, - proof of completeness, - a substitute for justification.
It is a supporting observation, not a requirement.


2.5.5 FAQ 4 — When is it acceptable not to claim saturation?
It is entirely acceptable not to claim saturation when: - access or time constraints limit further interviews, - the study is exploratory, - the aim is to capture key perspectives or roles, rather than exhaust a population.
In these cases, clarity about coverage is more important than invoking saturation.


2.5.6 FAQ 5 — What is one credible mitigation strategy?
Credible mitigation strategies include: - diversifying entry points for snowball sampling, - deliberately interviewing actors with different institutional roles or viewpoints, - triangulating interviews with documents, policy texts, or secondary data.


2.5.7 Model paragraph (acceptable at Master’s level)

“Interviews were conducted using a non-probability snowball sampling approach, appropriate given the limited visibility of the target population. Initial interviewees were selected to reflect different institutional roles, and subsequent referrals expanded coverage across perspectives. Data collection continued until no substantively new themes emerged in relation to implementation barriers, within the time and access constraints of the project. While the sample is not statistically representative, triangulation with documentary sources mitigates the risk of systematic bias.”







Examiner perspective



Examiners do not expect perfect samples. They look for judgement: whether the sampling choices are coherent, justified, and transparently linked to what the study can realistically achieve.




2.5.8 4.2 Quantitative / survey sampling (less common, but high-stakes when used)

2.5.8.1 Exemplar F — Simple random sampling (and what it implies)
Source: The contribution of social housing as physical capital… (Vienna), sampling and survey design (LE110 p. 16).
“A simple random sample… should represent the whole population… To keep the sampling error as small as possible a random sample selection was applied… meaning that every individual… had the same probability of being selected…” (LE110, p. 16)

FAQ prompts (answer in bullets): - What claim is the author trying to support by saying “random sample”? - What would you need to check (practically) before making that claim? - If your sample is not random, what should you write instead?


2.5.9 4.3 Special case exemplar: Commoning beyond Capitalism (why it is not a general template)
Some dissertations use a highly theory-driven qualitative approach and justify the methods through an explicit philosophical stance (e.g., critical realism). This can be excellent—but it is not always appropriate for every dissertation topic.

2.5.9.1 Exemplar G — Theory-driven interviewing + critical realism (special case)
Source: Hill, S. (2019). Commoning beyond Capitalism?, methodology sections on interviewing and critical realism (LE382, pp. 15–17).

“Organisations are best understood ‘through the experience of the individual people’… so interviews… are useful… Semi-structured interviews were chosen…” (LE382, p. 15)


“For the qualitative analysis, a critical realist method is utilised for two reasons: it does not have an ontologically reductive position and is theory-driven…” (LE382, p. 16)








Why this is a “special” exemplar



This dissertation is a strong model when your research question requires deep theory-driven interpretation and you can sustain that coherence throughout the thesis.
It is not a default template for more applied policy evaluation or data-constrained projects, where your Methods chapter should prioritise feasibility, access, and fit-for-purpose justification.


Your task (sampling paragraph draft): Write a 120–170 word sampling subsection for your dissertation, using the structure:

Population / unit of analysis

Sampling approach (and why)

Target sample size (and why)

Recruitment / access plan

Limitations + mitigation

title: Research Workshop: Literature Review (Students Driving, AI in the Back Seat)
text:
A literature review (LR) is a structured and critical account of what credible research has established about your topic, organised around an argument that supports your dissertation’s research objective(s).
It is not a “tour” of papers. It is a reasoned map: what we know, how we know it, what we do not know, and why your project is a logical next step.


A strong LR typically does three things simultaneously:

Defines the intellectual problem-space (concepts, theories, debates).
Synthesises evidence and approaches (patterns, tensions, boundary conditions).
Justifies your research objective(s) (gap + relevance + feasibility).







Your north star



Every paragraph should be able to answer:
“How does this revolves around or how connects with my research objective?”






A bibliography with sentences attached

A set of summaries (“Smith (2020) says…, Jones (2021) says…”)

A place to show you have read “a lot”

A proxy for your methodology or results

section: 2.1 The “analysis verbs” that change your writing
text:
2.1 The “analysis verbs” that change your writing
When you write, aim to do something with the literature. Use verbs that signal analytical moves:

Contrasts (A emphasises X, whereas B emphasises Y)
Qualifies (the effect holds when / if / provided that…)
Interrogates (questions assumptions, measures, identification)
Extends (applies ideas to a new context / population / time)
Integrates (combines two strands into a coherent framing)
Disentangles (separates mechanism from correlation)







A quick self-check



If your paragraph contains only verbs like describes, reports, notes, states, you are probably summarising rather than analysing.

title: Research Workshop: Literature Review (Students Driving, AI in the Back Seat)
section: 3.1 Task 1 — Spot the difference: summary vs analysis
text:
3.1 Task 1 — Spot the difference: summary vs analysis

3.1.1 Exemplar (descriptive vs analytical use of literature)
Source: Lumbe, L. (2021). The contribution of social housing as physical capital addressed in the “Smart City Wien Framework” to sustainable livelihoods.

“The definitions of ‘smart city’ could not be more different (Ponting, 2013)… Hence, there is no universally accepted description of this notion. For the purposes of this dissertation, Toli and Murtagh’s (2020) characterisation will be applied…” (Literature Review, pp. 7–8).

Why this is useful
This passage demonstrates careful coverage of definitions but only a light analytical intervention. It helps illustrate the boundary between high-quality description and explicit critical analysis.

Your task - Identify which sentences summarise existing work. - Identify where the author makes an analytical decision. - Rewrite one sentence to make the author’s judgement explicit.
crumbs: Research Workshop: Literature Review (Students Driving, AI in the Back Seat)

title: Research Workshop: Literature Review (Students Driving, AI in the Back Seat)
section: 3.2 Task 2 — Relevance filter (build judgement, not volume)
text:
3.2 Task 2 — Relevance filter (build judgement, not volume)

3.2.1 Exemplar (relevance-driven literature review)
Source: Bendavid, I. (2021). How travellers’ behaviour evolves with changes in shared e-scooter prices?

“E-scooters may be an effective solution to urban congestion and the last-mile problem. However, action must be taken for this new transport mode to better complement, rather than compete with sustainable modes of transport… This section will draw the evolution of research on micro-mobility, e-scooters and the microeconomics and marketing tools used in this paper.” (Literature Review, p. 7).

Why this is useful
The author clearly filters the literature through the research objective, demonstrating that relevance is defined by the research question, not by topic popularity.

Your task - Identify which strands of literature are prioritised. - Identify at least one plausible strand that is implicitly excluded. - Explain how this filtering supports the research objective.
crumbs: Research Workshop: Literature Review (Students Driving, AI in the Back Seat)

title: Research Workshop: Literature Review (Students Driving, AI in the Back Seat)
text:
3.3 Task 3 — One-sentence synthesis drill

3.3.1 Exemplar (synthesis across authors)
Source: Macpherson-Smith, E. (2021). Can urban regeneration unlock opportunities for women?

“Early feminist urban planning literature… was primarily focused on the needs of white middle-class women in the suburbs… Contemporary research led by Beebeejaun (2017) has instead attempted to reach historically marginalised women with a focus on intersectionality.” (Literature Review, pp. 7–8).

Why this is useful
This excerpt groups authors by intellectual position and evolution, rather than listing them individually. It is a clear example of synthesis.

Your task - Identify the organising principle used to group authors. - Write a one-sentence synthesis capturing the evolution of the debate. - Add a qualifier explaining why this evolution matters for the dissertation.
crumbs: Research Workshop: Literature Review (Students Driving, AI in the Back Seat)

title: Research Workshop: Literature Review (Students Driving, AI in the Back Seat)
section: 3.4 Task 3 — Name the gap type (stop vague “there is little literature” claims)
text:
3.4 Task 3 — Name the gap type (stop vague “there is little literature” claims)
Choose one paragraph from your current LR draft (or a sample you provide).
Identify the most relevant gap type:

Theoretical gap (missing mechanism or concept)
Methodological gap (identification, measurement, data limitations)
Contextual gap (different city/country/institutional setting)
Temporal gap (outdated period; post-policy change)
Population/heterogeneity gap (who is affected; distributional effects)

Write a 3–4 line gap statement that: 1. Names the gap type, 2. Explains why it matters, 3. Links directly to your objective.

3.4.1 Exemplar (a defensible research gap)
Source: Macpherson-Smith, E. (2021). Can urban regeneration unlock opportunities for women?

“Despite this recent emergence there are still significant gaps in feminist urban planning literature, with notable omissions in the study of regeneration and the lived experiences of inner-city women.” (Ibid, p. 7).

Why this is useful
The gap is defined as a systematic omission, not an absence of literature. This makes the gap credible and defensible.

Additional task - Identify the type of gap (contextual, population, methodological). - Explain why this gap matters for the research objective. - Rewrite the gap in one sentence without using “there is little research”.

title: Research Workshop: Literature Review (Students Driving, AI in the Back Seat)
section: 3.5 Task 5 — From literature to research design
text:
3.5 Task 5 — From literature to research design

3.5.1 Exemplar (literature review shaping method)
Source: Popham, E. (2021). Legislating for Sustainable Development Using Spatial Justice Principles.

“The aim of this literature review is to identify the spatial justice principles that are important to disrupt cycles of inequality… In order to establish an analytical framework… it is important to understand the key principles which represent spatial justice.” (Literature Review, pp. 8–9).

Why this is useful
This passage shows the literature review actively constructing the research framework, rather than serving as background.

Your task - Identify which concepts are carried forward into the framework. - Explain how theory is operationalised. - Suggest one alternative theory and how it would alter the research design.

title: Research Workshop: Literature Review (Students Driving, AI in the Back Seat)
section: 3.6 Task 6 — Paragraph surgery (rewrite with three constraints)
text:
3.6 Task 6 — Paragraph surgery (rewrite with three constraints)
Take a descriptive paragraph and rewrite it using:

1 analytical verb (e.g., qualifies, contrasts, interrogates)
1 explicit mechanism (the “because”)
1 bridge sentence back to your objective

Keep the paragraph within 120–160 words. ::: callout-tip ## Key takeaway
A strong literature review is not about demonstrating how much you have read. It is about demonstrating judgement: what matters, why it matters, and how it justifies the research you are about to undertake. :::

Use this as a self-audit before you submit a draft.

I have clear themes (not a chronological list of papers).

title: Research Workshop: Literature Review (Students Driving, AI in the Back Seat)
section: 3.11 A LR pipeline at a glance
text:
3.11 A LR pipeline at a glance
When writing a literature review remain compliant with University regulations on AI use.
The guiding principle is that AI may support research and reflection, but all assessed writing must be your own original work.
The core stages are:

Collect widely
Filter systematically
Read deeply (a minority of papers)
Map concepts and gaps
Design structure before writing
Write your own content
Review twice: diagnostic AI checks → full human review







Non-negotiable rule (assessment context)



AI tools may be used only as an aid to research, organisation, or reflection.
Under no circumstances should AI-generated text, structure, analysis, or paraphrased output be incorporated into assessed work.
You remain fully responsible for:

accuracy of claims,
interpretation of evidence,
correct citation,
coherence and logic linking the literature to your research objective.
crumbs: Research Workshop: Literature Review (Students Driving, AI in the Back Seat)

title: Research Workshop: Literature Review (Students Driving, AI in the Back Seat)
text:
3.12 Step 1 — Find literature (collect widely)

3.12.1 Goal
Build a broad, traceable, and defensible pool of candidate literature before deciding what merits close reading.


3.12.2 Tools (examples)

Reference manager: Zotero

Search & discovery: Google Scholar, Elicit, Consensus, Litmaps

Network discovery: Connected Papers, ResearchRabbit

Search/reading interfaces: SciSpace



3.12.3 What to do

Create a dedicated reference manager collection (e.g. Dissertation – Literature Review).
Search using topic terms + synonyms + methodological keywords.
Save all potentially relevant papers at this stage (do not over-filter early).
Record basic metadata:

topic/theme,
methods,
data/context,
key constructs or variables.








Old-school search still matters



iDiscover, Google Scholar remains valuable when you want full control over keywords and search logic.
AI tools complement this — they do not replace it.




3.12.4 Optional exercise (planning only)

Draft three keyword strings:

core topic terms,
methods/approaches,
context (place, time, population).

Use them in Google Scholar and one AI-assisted search tool, then import results into your reference manager.
crumbs: Research Workshop: Literature Review (Students Driving, AI in the Back Seat)

title: Research Workshop: Literature Review (Students Driving, AI in the Back Seat)
text:
3.13 Step 2 — Filter literature (triage, not judgement)

3.13.1 Goal
Reduce the reading burden by identifying papers most likely to matter for your research objective.


3.13.2 Tools (examples)

SciSpace (relevance indicators, filters)
Consensus (key papers, contributors, evidence clusters)
NotebookLM (querying your uploaded references)



3.13.3 What to do

Start from the full reference manager collection.
Use tools to assist screening, considering:

topical relevance,
alignment with your objective,
foundational vs. recent contributions.

Create three lists:

papers for full reading,
papers to revisit later,
papers excluded from this project.








AI assists triage, not judgement



AI can speed up screening, but you must still check titles, abstracts, and — where needed — methods or results sections yourself.
crumbs: Research Workshop: Literature Review (Students Driving, AI in the Back Seat)

title: Research Workshop: Literature Review (Students Driving, AI in the Back Seat)
section: 3.14 Step 3 — Full read (deep engagement with a subset)
text:
3.14 Step 3 — Full read (deep engagement with a subset)

3.14.1 Goal
Develop genuine understanding of the field without attempting to read everything.


3.14.2 Rule of thumb
After filtering, fully read around 20–25% of the shortlisted papers (those with highest signal value).


3.14.3 During a full read, extract (in your own notes)

research question and motivation,
theoretical mechanisms,
data and empirical strategy,
strengths and limitations,
key findings,
contribution relative to the literature,
unresolved issues or gaps.







This step cannot be automated



Skipping full reading risks misinterpretation, weak synthesis, and factual errors — all common triggers for academic misconduct investigations.
crumbs: Research Workshop: Literature Review (Students Driving, AI in the Back Seat)

title: Research Workshop: Literature Review (Students Driving, AI in the Back Seat)
text:
3.15 Step 4 — Mapping concepts and gaps

3.15.1 Goal
Transform a list of papers into a structured understanding of: - key concepts, - thematic groupings, - debates, - and research gaps linked to your objective.


3.15.2 Tools (examples)

NotebookLM (concept mapping / visual organisation)
Consensus (coverage matrices and gap indicators)



3.15.3 What to do

Build a conceptual map based on papers you have read.
Group literature by:

concepts or mechanisms,
methodological approaches,
contexts or datasets.

Identify:

areas of dense evidence,
contradictions,
under-explored questions.




3.15.4 Deliverable
A provisional set of themes and candidate sections, written in your own words.
crumbs: Research Workshop: Literature Review (Students Driving, AI in the Back Seat)

title: Research Workshop: Literature Review (Students Driving, AI in the Back Seat)
text:
3.16 Step 5 — Structure (design before drafting)

3.16.1 Goal
Design the architecture of the literature review before writing prose.


3.16.2 How to use AI (permitted)
AI may be used only to prompt reflection, not to generate a structure to reuse.
Acceptable use - asking for questions you should consider, - checking whether common elements are missing.
Not acceptable - copying AI-generated outlines into assessed work.






Structure must be yours



You must be able to justify: - why sections exist, - why they appear in that order, - how each section supports the research objective.




3.16.3 Example structure (illustrative, not prescriptive)

Framing the problem and relevance of the literature

Core concept/theme A

Core concept/theme B

Methodological or measurement issues (if relevant)

Debates and contested findings

Research gaps and positioning of your study

Summary and transition to research design

3.17 Step 6 — Content (authorial control)

3.17.1 Goal
Write the literature review entirely in your own words, grounded in sources you have read.


3.17.2 Permitted AI support

clarifying terminology,
checking logical consistency,
identifying where citations may be needed,
locating additional sources you then read yourself.



3.17.3 Writing discipline
Each paragraph should contain: - a clear claim, - supporting evidence (citations), - interpretation or comparison, - explicit relevance to the research objective.






Literature reviews are analytical, not descriptive



Avoid paper-by-paper summaries. Focus on synthesis, comparison, and evaluation.

title: Research Workshop: Literature Review (Students Driving, AI in the Back Seat)
text:
3.18 Step 7 — Review (diagnostic AI → manual review)

3.18.1 Diagnostic AI checks (permitted)
AI may be used to flag risks, not to rewrite text.
Examples of acceptable checks: - alignment with learning outcomes, - missing citations, - unclear definitions, - logical gaps.






Treat AI feedback as a checklist



AI suggestions are prompts for your judgement — not instructions to implement verbatim.




3.18.2 Manual review (mandatory)

Read every sentence critically.
Check coherence, argument flow, and citation accuracy.
Proofread carefully.



3.18.3 Two manual lenses

Academic rigor: is the argument defensible and evidence-based?

Readability: is the text clear, precise, and error-free?







Peer review strengthens integrity



Feedback from supervisors, postdocs, or senior PhD students can reveal weaknesses early and reduce risk later.

3.19 Permitted prompt examples (planning and checking only)

3.19.1 Prompt A — Screening checklist

My research objective is [insert].
Based on these titles/abstracts [paste], generate a screening checklist I should apply myself when deciding what to read fully.
Do not summarise or evaluate individual papers.



3.19.2 Prompt B — Structure reflection

My research objective is [insert].
Generate questions that would help me design a logical literature review structure.
Do not propose headings or an outline.



3.19.3 Prompt C — Risk audit

Here is my draft and the marking criteria.
Identify risk areas only (e.g. unsupported claims, missing citations, unclear positioning).
Do not rewrite or suggest replacement text.

3.20 What “success” looks like
A strong literature review: - is organised around themes and mechanisms, - demonstrates critical evaluation, - clearly supports the research objective, - ends with a well-justified research gap.

3.21 Academic integrity reminder

AI output must never appear in assessed work (directly or paraphrased).
AI may be used for research assistance, planning, and self-checking only.
All claims must be verified against original sources.
You may be required to declare AI use and defend your work in a viva.







Policy takes precedence



Always follow module-specific and departmental guidance.
If in doubt, seek clarification before submission.
